title: Modeling Financial Literacy Through Explainable Machine Learning and Behavioral Segmentation in Emerging Economies
authors: Chowdhury, T.; Chowdhury, M.; Rahman, M.; Ahmed, I.; Ahmed, N.; Tuhin, M.; Kafy, A.
tldr: Uses Random Forest, XGBoost, and k-means clustering on 1067 Bangladeshi adults to identify three financial behavioral segments and key literacy predictors including institutional trust.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional demographic methods fail to capture the complexity of digital financial behavior in emerging economies. Understanding how individuals use financial technology is limited, hampering the design of effective interventions for diverse populations.
approach: Surveyed 1067 adults in Bangladesh using structured financial literacy assessment.
Applied Random Forest and XGBoost for classification with SHAP analysis for interpretability.
Used k-means clustering (validated with silhouette 0.42, Davies-Bouldin 1.08, Calinski-Harabasz 287.3) for behavioral segmentation.
Compared demographics, behavioral, and attitudinal predictors of financial literacy.
Evaluated with F1-score and 58% improvement over random guessing baseline.
findings: num: Achieved F1-score of 0.52, a 58% improvement over random guessing.
num: Institutional trust (importance 0.18) outperformed education (0.09) as a predictor.
Three behavioral segments: Digitally Literate Planners (34%, knowledge 7.8/10), Informally Active Underskilled (41%, 5.4/10), Digitally Excluded Traditionalists (25%, 3.1/10).
num: Rural users had 7.3% higher financial literacy than urban users.
Formal education did not significantly impact financial literacy levels.
Weak correlations between financial knowledge and actual behaviors (coefficients below 0.10).

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study demonstrates that machine learning methods can identify behavioral financial literacy segments in emerging economies that traditional demographic analysis would miss. It reveals that institutional trust is a stronger predictor of financial literacy than education, and that rural users exhibit higher literacy than urban users. The three-segment framework (Digitally Literate Planners, Informally Active Underskilled, Digitally Excluded Traditionalists) provides a behavioral basis for targeted financial education interventions.
directly_justifies: Institutional trust (importance 0.18) outperforms education (0.09) as literacy predictor.
Rural users show 7.3% higher financial literacy than urban users in Bangladesh.
Weak correlations (below 0.10) between financial knowledge and actual behaviors.
limits: Self-reported survey data may not reflect actual financial behaviors.
Bangladesh-specific sample limits generalizability to other emerging economies.
Moderate clustering validity (silhouette 0.42) suggests overlapping segments.
